The search turned up useful o200k_base measurements, but almost nothing measured for Claude's tokenizer, so I can't give you a reliable Claude ratio.

**o200k_base (GPT-4o)**
- One small test with eight meaning-matched Korean/English pairs found Korean needing about 1.3x as many tokens on average, ranging from roughly 1.09x to 1.42x. Technical paragraphs showed the largest gap. The mean ratio was 1.30x (median 1.33x, range 1.09x to 1.42x). This is a small sample, and the source is a vendor blog.
- A larger test covered 285 articles published in Korean, Japanese, English, and Chinese, tokenized with o200k_base, cl100k_base, and Claude's tokenizer. Its headline figure is that Korean ran 1.38x English tokens, Japanese 1.34x. The snippet doesn't say which tokenizer produced that number, so treat it as an aggregate across tokenizers rather than an o200k-specific figure.
- An academic paper (ICICPE 2024) also measures a "Korean penalty" for several tokenizers, using the FLORES-200 parallel corpus. Its results indicate a linear increase in the disadvantage faced by Korean text as the Korean/English character length ratio rises. The snippet I retrieved doesn't include its specific o200k or Claude numbers, so check the full paper.

**Claude's tokenizer**
- The only Claude-specific numbers are estimates. A GitHub-style feature request gives rough counts such as "Refactor this function" (English) ~4 tokens; "이 함수를 리팩토링해줘" (Korean) ~10–14 tokens, and concludes that Korean users consume roughly 2x–3x more tokens. Those figures are approximate and unmeasured.
- A general comparison notes that the same sentence produces 6 tokens in GPT-4, 7 in Claude 3, and 8 in Llama 2. That is an English example, so it doesn't settle the Korean question for Claude.

**Conflicting figures**
- Estimates range widely. One blog post claims that every Korean translation costs approximately 2.8x the English equivalent. The other sources I found put the ratio between about 1.3x and 2x. The gap likely depends on the text, since denser technical writing and per-character comparisons come out higher than short, conversational sentences.

**Bottom line:** For o200k_base, a Korean-to-English ratio of roughly 1.3–1.4x in tokens is the best-supported figure from these results. For Claude, I found no reliable measurement. To get your own number, run the same paired texts through tiktoken's o200k_base encoding and the Hugging Face Xenova/claude-tokenizer, which one of the sources used. Keep in mind that the Xenova tokenizer is a community port, so it may not exactly match Anthropic's current tokenizer.

I found several sources on this, but none is a head-to-head study of Claude and OpenAI tokenizers on Korean and English. The closest evidence comes from a blog measurement and a Korean-authored paper.

**Academic and technical sources**

- **Korean penalty (Korea University, 2024):** Researchers found that among four large language models, including GPT-4, processing Korean requires up to three times more tokens than processing English. They argue this implies higher costs and slower processing speeds for tasks performed in Korean.
- **A.X K1 technical report (2026):** This report compares its own tokenizer with OpenAI's o200k and Qwen3. For Korean general text, the average is 526.72 tokens for A.X K1, 811.71 for OpenAI o200k, and 905.82 for Qwen3. For English general text, the figures are 792.28 for A.X K1, 769.31 for OpenAI o200k, and 794.79 for Qwen3. So o200k is slightly more efficient than the others on English, but it still uses far more tokens on Korean. Note that this report does not include a Claude tokenizer.
- **Language-specific tokenizer study (Seoul National University):** This paper studies how a Korean-extended tokenizer changes model behavior compared with a basic English-centric tokenizer, but it does not address Claude or OpenAI directly. It explores how language-specific tokenizers influence the behavior of Large Language Models predominantly trained with English text data, through the case study of Korean.

**Claude vs. OpenAI measurement (blog, not peer-reviewed)**

A blog post (jangwook.net) measured the same parallel corpus across tokenizers. Its findings:
- Even on the modern tokenizer (o200k), Korean is 1.38x English and Japanese 1.34x.
- On the Claude tokenizer, Korean is the most expensive of the three at 1.88x.
- In a single-sentence example, the same Korean sentence is 20 on o200k and 32 on Claude. This suggests Claude's tokenizer is noticeably less efficient than o200k for Korean, though this is one author's measurement on one corpus.

**Other sources (lower reliability)**

- A DEV Community article reports a Korean token premium but was measured with tiktoken o200k_base as a documented proxy because the ratio is tokenizer-stable. It recommends that for exact per-request counts on Claude, call the count_tokens API. That's a useful practical step if you need exact numbers.
- A GitHub-style feature request claims Korean users burn through Claude usage limits 2–3x faster, but its token counts are described only as approximate and it is a user complaint rather than a study.
- A blog on tokenization reports that Korean costs 2.8x, Japanese 2.4x, and Traditional Chinese 2.1x more tokens per post, based on the author's own translated posts.

**Bottom line:** Korean consistently needs roughly 1.4x to 3x more tokens than English, depending on the tokenizer and the test. OpenAI's o200k is more efficient for Korean than older OpenAI tokenizers and, in one comparison, than Claude's. Exact ratios for Claude vary by source, and no rigorous, peer-reviewed Claude-vs-OpenAI Korean comparison appeared in these results. If you need precise figures for your own content, measure with the official token counting tools.

content.text:
Las cifras dependen mucho del tokenizador y del tipo de texto. No encontré ningún estudio revisado por pares que compare directamente OpenAI y Claude en coreano frente a inglés, así que lo que sigue es lo mejor que hay en fuentes públicas.

## Cifras principales

| Tokenizador | Coreano / inglés (mismo texto) | Fuente |
|---|---|---|
| **OpenAI o200k_base** (GPT‑4o y posteriores) | **≈1,38×** | Blog de jangwook.net, corpus paralelo de 285 artículos |
| **OpenAI o200k_base** | **≈1,30×** de media (rango 1,09×–1,42×; mediana 1,33×) | DEV Community, 8 pares de frases equivalentes |
| **OpenAI cl100k_base** (GPT‑4 / GPT‑3.5) | **hasta ~3×** | Korea University, ICICPE 2024 (corpus FLORES‑200) |
| **Claude** | **≈1,88×** | jangwook.net (mismo corpus que la fila del o200k) |
| **Claude** (estimación de un usuario) | **~2–3×** | Petición de funcionalidad #26401 (cifras aproximadas, sin medición rigurosa) |

Un ejemplo concreto de jangwook.net: la misma frase en coreano ocupa **20 tokens con o200k y 32 con Claude**.

## Matices importantes

- **OpenAI mejoró mucho con o200k.** Con el tokenizador antiguo, cl100k (GPT‑4), el coreano llegaba a necesitar unas 3 veces más tokens. Con o200k la diferencia baja a unas 1,3–1,4 veces.
- **La cifra de Claude es la menos fiable.** Sale del blog de una sola persona, no revisado por pares. Además, Anthropic no publica su tokenizador. Esas mediciones suelen usar `Xenova/claude-tokenizer`, una versión de la comunidad que puede no coincidir con el tokenizador de los modelos actuales de Claude. Para cifras exactas, usa el endpoint oficial `count_tokens` de la API de Anthropic.
- **Depende del tipo de texto.** Los textos técnicos dan las diferencias más grandes. El paper de Korea University muestra que la desventaja crece de forma lineal con la proporción de longitud en caracteres entre coreano e inglés.
- **Hay cifras más altas por ahí,** como 2,8× en [blakecrosley.com](https://blakecrosley.com/blog/tokenization-visualizer). Suelen venir de traducciones propias o de muestras pequeñas.
- El informe técnico A.X K1 (2026) da para o200k unos 812 tokens de media en textos generales en coreano y unos 769 en inglés. No parecen textos paralelos, así que no sirve como ratio directa.

**Resumen:** con OpenAI (o200k), el coreano necesita entre un 30 % y un 40 % más de tokens que el inglés. Con Claude, la única medición pública indica cerca de un 90 % más (≈1,9×), con poca certeza. Si te importa el coste real, mide tus propios textos con `tiktoken` (o200k_base) y con `count_tokens` de Anthropic.

Fuentes:
- [The Non-English Token Tax — Korean Costs 1.4x, Measured (jangwook.net)](https://jangwook.net/en/blog/en/multilingual-llm-token-tax-experiment/)
- [Korean vs English: do you pay more tokens for the same prompt? (DEV Community)](https://dev.to/claudeguide/korean-vs-english-do-you-pay-more-tokens-for-the-same-prompt-jm8)
- [Korean Penalty of Large Language Models Derived by the Tokenizer, ICICPE 2024 (Korea University)](https://hiai.korea.ac.kr/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/Korean-Penalty-of-Large-Language-Models-Derived-by-the-Tokenizer_ICICPE_2024.pdf)
- [A.X K1 Technical Report (arXiv)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2601.09200)
- [How does a Language-Specific Tokenizer affect LLMs? (arXiv)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2502.12560)
- [Feature request #26401: Non-English users (Korean/Japanese/CJK) face structural disadvantage](https://claudeissues.com/issue/26401-feature-request-non-english-users-korean-japanese-cjk-face-structural-disadvanta)
- [Tokenization visualizer (blakecrosley.com)](https://blakecrosley.com/blog/tokenization-visualizer)
